messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Conflict: Confrontations, Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

It was a Tuesday night in late November when the relationship that Mark had believed was built on trust finally showed its true shape. His partner, Lisa, had been drinking again, and what started as a sharp exchange over money escalated in the way it always did—her voice rising, her face hardening—but that night something was different. She had been cooking, and in the heat of her anger she swept the frying pan off the stove, sending oil and a half-charred piece of chicken across the linoleum. The smell was acrid, burnt, and it filled the small kitchen so completely that Mark thought for a moment he was on fire himself. She came at him then, fists closed, and he did not fight back. He had never fought back. What stayed with him afterward was not just the shock of the blows, but that oily, burnt smell that seemed to cling to his clothes, his hair, his skin for days. He left the apartment that night, never returned, and the relationship ended within a month, but the burnt smell never really left.

For the first several weeks, Mark could not bear to drive past the building where it happened. He took a different route to work, adding twenty minutes to his commute, and told himself it was because of traffic. He also found that he could not think about that night without his chest tightening and his hands growing clammy, so he simply did not think about it. He kept his mind busy with work, with television, with anything that did not lead back to that kitchen. But the thoughts had a way of ambushing him anyway, especially at night. When his head hit the pillow, the memory was waiting. So Mark started staying up late, sometimes until two or three in the morning, watching late-night infomercials or scrolling through his phone until exhaustion finally took him. His wife, Rachel, noticed that he rarely came to bed with her anymore, but he told her his back hurt from crouching under sinks all day, and she accepted it.

The triggers that caught him off guard were the hardest. As a plumber, Mark spent his days in basements and crawl spaces where smells collected. A burnt-out water heater, a shorted wire, or even the faint scorch of a furnace pilot light could stop him mid-motion, his breath gone, his mind suddenly back in that kitchen. He learned to pause, to take slow breaths, but the wave always came first. Worse were the confrontations. A customer who raised his voice over a slow drain, a supervisor who spoke sharply about a missed call—any expression of anger, even the calm, measured kind, sent Mark into a quiet panic. He had come to believe that anger, no matter who was holding it, was the first step toward something violent. He began avoiding customers he knew were upset, letting his apprentice handle the tough calls, and he never contradicted anyone, even when he was right. His work suffered in small ways—he took longer on jobs, he double-checked everything—but he managed.

What finally brought Mark to seek help was a moment at a hardware store. A man ahead of him in line began complaining loudly about the price of pipe fittings, his face reddening, his voice rising. Mark felt the familiar tightness in his throat, the heat behind his eyes, and he set down his items and walked out of the store without buying anything. He stood in the parking lot, trembling, and realized he had been doing that more and more—leaving situations before the anger could fully arrive, before he could be hurt again. His wife had noticed, too, and had asked him gently what was wrong. He could not tell her. But later that night, unable to sleep, he searched online for a counselor who dealt with trauma. He is afraid that talking about it will make it real all over again, but he is also afraid of continuing to slip away from his own life, one avoided conversation at a time.
